spans.s:
ekoddiṣṭa
(‘intended for one’)
------------------------------------------
Performance of certain religious rites for the peace of the सोउल् of a dead person is an ancient custom in almost all religions and cultures of the world. In हिन्दुइस्म्, such rites are called by the general term ‘śrāddha.’
Generally such śrāddhas are performed for the three (dead) paternal ancestors of a person and are termed ‘pārvaṇaśrāddha.’
The एकोद्दिष्ट śrāddha, on the other hand, is performed only for the benefit of one person, who has just passed away (eka = one, uddiṣṭa = intended for).
This rite is done throughout one year after death. After that, the dead person attains the realm of his forefathers through the special ritual of ‘sapiṇḍī-karaṇa’. (See SAPIṆḌĪKARAṆA for details.)
In this śrāddha there is no offering of cooked ड़ोओद् or आज्य (ghee) to be offered into the fire (called अग्नौकरण). There is no invitation to the ब्राह्मणस् to represent the Viśvedevās. The mantras uttered and the questions asked of the other ब्राह्मणस् are also different.
An uneven number of ब्राह्मणस् are fed on the eleventh day.
See also ŚRĀDDHA.
